title: Wiki for Human Rights Nigeria: Wiki Leadership Training, Electoral Integrity Training, End-of-Year Fiscal Meeting, and October Physical Meetup
content: From August to September, I participated in the WLX Initiative programme organized by Wikimedia Nigeria and a Nigerian consulting firm, Knewrow. When I was selected to be part of the programme, I knew it was a four-week programme, but I didn’t know what it entailed until I became involved in the series of virtual sessions, assignments, and projects. Out of more than 50 participants, I emerged as one of the top five, behind the overall winner, who received a scholarship to Wiki Indaba. The four-week programme leaned heavily on leadership learning moments and reflections. The virtual sessions covered topics on leadership beyond contribution, personal accountability and ownership, communication and community engagement, mentorship and leadership replication, sustainability, social responsibility and community growth, and collaboration and conflict resolution.

title: Preserving Irra’s Heritage, Empowering Its Youth: AIHI and Yoruba Wikipedia Fan Club Offa Train Community Youths Ahead of Oya Festival 2026
content:
The preservation of our cultural heritage begins with the people who own the stories, traditions, and histories. As communities continue to embrace digital technologies, it is increasingly important to equip young people with the knowledge and skills to document, preserve, and share their cultural heritage with the world.

In a significant step towards achieving this, the African Institute for Heritage Intelligence (AIHI), in collaboration with Yoruba Wikipedia Fan Club Offa, organised a one-day digital heritage documentation and Wikimedia training for youths and students in Irra community, ahead of the highly anticipated Oya Festival 2026.

The training was held at the Onira Palace, Irra, providing an important cultural setting for the engagement. Bringing the training to the palace was particularly meaningful, as it connected the younger generation directly with the traditional institution and the cultural heritage they are being empowered to document and preserve.

title: Along the Red Sea Coast: Documenting the Heritage of Hurghada and El Qoseir
content:
From 10 to 12 October 2026, six members of the Egypt Wikimedians User Group embarked on a three-day photo documentation trip to Hurghada and El Qoseir, two coastal cities whose heritage extends far beyond their familiar image as tourist destinations. The expedition explored historic neighbourhoods, museums, scientific institutions, religious landmarks, and industrial remains, documenting the region’s diverse cultural and natural heritage. Through photography and subsequent editorial work, the participants sought to address gaps in the representation of these places across Wikimedia projects and make the history of these places more accessible through freely available knowledge.


The first two days focused on Hurghada, a city shaped by its relationship with the Red Sea, its maritime environment, and the growth of tourism. Rather than focusing solely on its resorts and beaches, the six participants explored several aspects of the city’s urban, cultural, and scientific heritage. The participants were Amr Fathy, Donia El Domiaty, Sohila El Shaer, Summer Kamal, Mohamed Ouda, and Ibrahim El Aidy.

title: Wikimedia at the World Shakespeare Congress in Verona
content: From 20 to 26 July 2026, Verona hosted the 12th World Shakespeare Congress, organised by the International Shakespeare Association as part of its 50th-anniversary celebrations. The theme chosen for this edition, Planetary Shakespeares, invited scholars from around the world to reflect on the role of Shakespeare’s works in the face of today’s cultural, social, and technological transformations. Within the Congress’s wide-ranging programme, two initiatives placed Wikimedia projects in the spotlight, highlighting their contribution to research, teaching, and the dissemination of free knowledge.

title: Kochi, from the inside: what it really takes to run WikiConference India 2026
content:
Most people meet a conference on its first morning: a badge, a lanyard, a full hall. I met WikiConference India 2026 six months earlier, in a shared document full of half-written page sections, translation drafts and a long list of questions that nobody had answered yet.

From 4 to 6 September 2026, WikiConference India 2026 brought Wikimedians from across the country to Kochi under the theme Reimagining the Knowledge Commons. I was there on a full scholarship, as a Core Team Member of the Communications Sub-team, as an on-site volunteer, and as a lightning-talk speaker. This post is about the part of a conference that rarely makes it into the photographs: the work before it, the work during it, and what I learned from both.

I joined the Communications Sub-team on 28 March 2026, in the group that looked after the conference pages on Meta-Wiki. It sounds like a small job. It is not. For most people, the Meta-Wiki page is the conference until the day they arrive. It is where they learn the theme, the dates, how to submit a session, how to apply for a scholarship and what to expect.

title: Celebrating 14 Years of Wikidata: Global WikiEducation Initiative Brings Tanzania’s Open Knowledge Community Together
content: In October 2026, Global WikiEducation Initiative (GWEI), with the support of Wikimedia Deutschland, joined the global Wikimedia community in celebrating the 14th birthday of Wikidata through a community event held in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The celebration brought together Wikimedians and people interested in open knowledge to recognise Wikidata’s contribution to making information freely accessible, structured and reusable around the world. The event was not only an opportunity to celebrate another year of Wikidata but also a moment to reflect on the importance of documenting local knowledge, improving the visibility of African contributions and encouraging more people to participate in the open knowledge movement.

content:
Latest tech news from the Wikimedia technical community. Please tell other users about these changes. Not all changes will affect you. Translations are available.

Updates for editors

  • At wikis where Mentorship is configured, permanently blocked users will no longer be assigned a new mentor when their original mentor quits. Temporarily blocked users will still be assigned a new mentor, in line with existing Mentorship practices. [1]
  • VisualEditor’s citation tool will be changed later this week to always open the “automatic” tab (Citoid) instead of remembering the last tab used by an editor. This change is made to support inexperienced editors who rely on the automatic citation option to create references, but often struggle to find it again after clicking on the “manual” or “re-use” tab. title: The people behind the Portuguese-language Wikipedia: stories from Brazil’s Wikimedia community
content:
The Portuguese-language Wikipedia was the third edition of the project to go live, just four months after the launch of the global initiative. This year, we are celebrating not only the platform’s longevity, but also the strength and resilience of a diverse community of volunteer contributors who, since 2001, have worked to make knowledge on the Portuguese-speaking internet increasingly free, accessible, and verifiable.

As part of an effort to recognize and celebrate this community, Wikimedia Brasil interviewed contributors from different professional backgrounds, areas of expertise, and fields of interest, compiling their stories in the e-book Wikipedia at 25 – Meet the people behind the encyclopedia (in Portuguese). The publication aims to raise awareness of the human foundation of the Wiki ecosystem. It is through people’s voluntary and collaborative engagement that the processes of writing, editing, debating, and assessing the notability and accuracy of content on the platform take place. Technology is built on knowledge, and knowledge is human.

title: Wikipedia, historical knowledge and the classroom
content:
Over the past decade and more, there’s been much enthusiasm around integrating Wikipedia into Higher Education teaching. Since 2017, we, as two academic historians based in the UK, have worked together to integrate Wikipedia into our pedagogy at the Universities of Sheffield, Edinburgh, and Glasgow, both in person and online, and across undergraduate and postgraduate levels. We have trained over one hundred students to become Wikipedia editors, and they have updated a whole host of historical articles on the platform to reflect up-to-date scholarship (for example these), not to mention the exercise’s benefits to students’ understanding of public history, as already noted by Charles West in 2018. 

We are far from alone from using Wikipedia as another pedagogical resource, as demonstrated by a Wikimedia in Education report, co-produced with the University of Edinburgh, and the increasing number of courses listed in the Wiki Education Dashboard.

title: The First Step Toward Ethical AI Edit
content:
From science to art and every discipline in between have felt the impact of Artificial Intelligence. Some cheerfully welcome the changing landscape; yet some get blindsided and left struggling on the track.

However, Pandora’s Box, once open, cannot be closed again; whether you like it or not, Artificial Intelligence is here to stay, and thus we need to face it.

This is the background which the event commenced; Indigenous Wikipedia and Artificial Intelligence Workshop is a special occurrence initiated by Wikimedia Foundation and Ministry of Education, co-headed by Wikidata Taiwan Community and Se-cyun Wikipidiya Seediq to lead the discussion on the contemporary challenges and explore the opportunities and concerns with the community. One of which is that, Large Language Models (LLMs) which consist of basically all the AI products on the market today, can very easily generate English and Chinese content at lightning speed, and more terrifying is that they are improving at an even higher speed. At the current state, most of the free-tier services already possess the capability to generate a full, syntactically correct Wikipedia article on their own.

title: Preserving Nepal’s Cultural Heritage Through Open Knowledge: Wiki Loves Monuments 2026
content:
Community-led photography, digital innovation and strategic partnerships are connecting Nepal’s historic monuments with a global audience.

Nepal’s cultural heritage from ancient temples and historic palaces to traditional courtyards and intricate stone sculptures reflects centuries of artistic achievement, cultural traditions and collective memory. Documenting and sharing this heritage is essential to increasing public awareness and ensuring that knowledge remains accessible to future generations.

Wiki Loves Monuments 2026 in Nepal, coordinated by Wikimedians of Nepal with UNESCO as a strategic partner, brought together photographers, volunteers, heritage enthusiasts and partner organizations to document Nepal’s built heritage and make photographs freely accessible worldwide.

Held from 1 September to 15 October 2026, the campaign demonstrated how community participation, photography and open knowledge can complement efforts to promote cultural heritage awareness and digital documentation.
snippet: Community-led photography, digital innovation and strategic partnerships are connecting Nepal’s historic monuments with a global audience.
creator: Nabin K. Sapkota

title: Tools don’t die from bugs: what thousands of Toolforge tools reveal about how Wikimedia runs
content:
Every day, a large share of the work on Wikimedia projects is done not by people typing into an edit box but by tools: bots that fix links, scripts that import data, dashboards that track campaigns, web tools that editors open dozens of times a week. Most of them live on Toolforge, the shared hosting platform where volunteers build and run software for the movement.

For Wikimania 2026 in Paris, I wanted to answer a question that sounds simple: how many of these tools exist, how many still work, and how would anyone find the right one? The result was a research poster, Mapping Toolforge: A Visual Ecosystem of Wikimedia Tools, presented in the poster session on 23 July 2026. This post summarises what the data showed, where the numbers have limits, and what I think should happen next.

The question came out of building WhichTool, a search layer that lets an editor describe a task and find a suitable tool. Before I could rank tools, I needed to know which ones were still alive. Nobody seemed to have that answer in one place.

title: Wikimedians-in-Residence at Indian Institute of Technology Delhi: Our Journey So Far
content:
After a lot of procrastinating today, I’m finally sitting down to write this blog.

In my previous blog, I shared that IIT Delhi has become the first IIT in India to start a GLAM-Wiki initiative, and appoint two Wikimedians-in-Residence .This time, I want to talk about what we have actually done so far and where we want to go next.

We began with the library staff. While planning, we noticed that many people mix up Wikimedia and Wikipedia, so we decided to clear that up first by holding a workshop on Wikimedia and its sister projects.

We discussed the idea with the librarian, then agreed on a date and time. The workshop was scheduled for Library Week. The library had also planned an educational visit to the Sonipat campus and Ashoka University, so we joined the trip, explored the campus, and held the workshop at Ashoka University. The slides below were presented during this workshop.

We explained what Wikimedia is, how Wikipedia and the other sister projects fit in, and how people can use them in daily life. The main point we wanted to get across was that Wikimedia is much more than Wikipedia.

title: Whose Knowledge Gets Counted? Fourteen Years of Wikidata and African Women’s Contributions
content:
For fourteen years, Wikidata has helped organise the world’s knowledge into a structured, interconnected and freely accessible resource. From people and institutions to languages, cultural heritage and historical events, its data connects information across languages and digital platforms.

Yet, as Wikidata celebrates its 14th birthday and enters its fifteenth year, an important question remains: whose knowledge is being documented, whose contributions are visible, and who gets to participate in shaping the knowledge systems increasingly influencing how we discover and understand the world?

For African Wiki Women, this question goes beyond the absence of biographies or incomplete records. It concerns their participation in the processes through which knowledge is sourced, organised, connected and made accessible.

title: From a rejected applicant to the Mentor Summit: Wikimedia at Google Summer of Code 2026
content:
📷 Featured image: GSoC Mentor Summit 2026 group photo

In 2018, I applied to Google Summer of Code but wasn’t selected. The next year I reapplied and got selected as a GSoC contributor. I then continued my role as a contributor and mentor and now I have gone on to be Wikimedia’s organisation administrator and then I have represented Wikimedia at GSoC Mentor Summit.

My first summit experience was in 2023, and after some change of plans I had the privilege of returning to my second in Munich, Germany. From 30 October – 1 November 2026, I joined Sarthak Parashar as one of two representatives to meet mentors and org admins of more than 100 open source communities.

All below is a summary of what we discussed, what other communities are facing and what I think should be brought back to Wikimedia.

This is unlike any conference. As a full unconference, there isn’t a set programme in advance. Any mentor or org admin can submit a session by adding a sticky note to the schedule board and the rest of us choose what sessions to attend. We filled the entire schedule by the first morning, which shows what’s currently on people’s minds.
